page.mentor_intro: Most low back pain is mechanical and self-limiting; the clinician's job is to find the small fraction that is not. Red flags — cancer history, fever, weight loss, night pain, neurological deficit, bowel/bladder dysfunction — are the screening grammar, and guideline reviews show which flags are actually endorsed and with what strength. The sobering evidence: individual red flags have weak diagnostic accuracy, so clustering and judgment matter more than any single question. Inflammatory back pain suggests axial spondyloarthritis — age under 40-45, insidious onset, morning stiffness, improvement with activity, alternating buttock pain — where early MRI and rheumatology referral change outcomes, while MRI for uncomplicated mechanical pain correlates poorly with symptoms and invites overtreatment.

teaching_points.claim: Most low back pain is mechanical/nonspecific; red flags are the screening tool for serious pathology (malignancy, infection, fracture, cauda equina), and their presence — not pain severity — drives imaging and referral.

Guideline reviews show variable endorsement of red flags; individual flags have limited diagnostic accuracy in emergency-department cohorts, so clusters of findings and clinical context must guide decisions.

Inflammatory back pain (insidious onset before 40-45, morning stiffness >30-60 minutes, improvement with exercise not rest, alternating buttock pain, night waking) suggests axial spondyloarthritis and warrants inflammatory work-up and appropriate imaging.

MRI is indicated for red flags, suspected cauda equina, infection, or inflammatory disease — not for uncomplicated mechanical pain, where degenerative findings are common in asymptomatic people and correlate poorly with symptoms.

uncertainties: Optimal combinations and weighting of red flags for screening rules is not settled across guidelines.
When to refer possible axial spondyloarthritis with negative imaging (non-radiographic disease) follows expert frameworks rather than trial evidence.
mcq_angles: Red-flag clusters and their limited individual accuracy.
Cauda equina red flags and urgent-MRI thresholds.

Appropriate versus inappropriate MRI indications.

page.mentor_intro: Antiviral treatment of influenza is a timing and selection problem. Oseltamivir remains the workhorse neuraminidase inhibitor, ideally started within 48 hours of symptom onset, with benefit extending beyond that window in severe or progressive disease; baloxavir added a single-dose polymerase-acid-inhibitor option. The 2024 network meta-analyses for WHO guidance rank the options separately for severe and nonsevere influenza — an important distinction because evidence and effect sizes differ by severity. Hospitalised and high-risk patients should be treated regardless of illness duration; the '48-hour rule' is a community outpatient rule, not a hospital one.

teaching_points.claim: Neuraminidase inhibitors (oseltamivir oral, zanamivir inhaled, peramivir IV) and the cap-dependent endonuclease inhibitor baloxavir are the available classes; oseltamivir is the standard for most patients.
Treatment within 48 hours of symptom onset maximises benefit in outpatient influenza; hospitalised, severe, or high-risk patients should be treated even beyond 48 hours.
Network meta-analysis for severe influenza supports oseltamivir-based regimens as the evidence-backed choice, with other classes positioned by severity and resistance patterns.
For nonsevere influenza, comparative effectiveness across agents is modest; single-dose baloxavir offers adherence advantages in selected patients.

uncertainties: Whether combination antiviral therapy adds benefit in severe influenza is untested adequately.
Baloxavir resistance (PA/I38 substitutions) and its clinical significance are evolving concerns.
mcq_angles: Antiviral classes, mechanisms, and resistance.

page.mentor_intro: This topic pairs the two halves of influenza control: vaccination as prevention, and neuraminidase-inhibitor prophylaxis as the pharmacological bridge. Annual vaccination is recommended for high-risk groups — older adults, chronic disease, pregnancy, immunosuppression — and meta-analysis confirms effectiveness against laboratory-confirmed illness, though effectiveness varies by season, match, and group. Chemoprophylaxis with oseltamivir after exposure reduces symptomatic influenza in the unvaccinated and outbreak settings; it complements, never replaces, vaccination. The mature clinical skill is timing: vaccinate before the season, treat within 48 hours, and prophylax only where guidelines indicate.

teaching_points.claim: Annual influenza vaccination is recommended for high-risk groups (age 65+, chronic cardiopulmonary disease, diabetes, pregnancy, immunosuppression, healthcare workers); healthy-adult benefit is mainly work-loss reduction.

Meta-analysis confirms vaccine effectiveness in high-risk groups, though magnitude varies by season and match — protection is real but partial, which is why high-risk patients still need early antiviral treatment when ill.
Neuraminidase-inhibitor post-exposure prophylaxis (oseltamivir) reduces symptomatic influenza after exposure; network meta-analysis supports NIs over other classes for prophylaxis.
Antiviral treatment should not wait for vaccine protection decisions: vaccinated or not, high-risk patients with influenza symptoms warrant early oseltamivir within 48 hours.

uncertainties: Optimal vaccine composition strategies (egg versus cell versus recombinant; high-dose/adjuvanted for older adults) continue to evolve with effectiveness data.
Duration and indications for extended prophylaxis in immunocompromised patients are not standardised.

page.mentor_intro: SMART — single maintenance and reliever therapy — is the most important asthma strategy shift of the GINA era: one inhaler, low-dose inhaled corticosteroid-formoterol, serves as daily preventer and as-needed reliever, guaranteeing an anti-inflammatory dose with every reliever use. Evidence shows fewer severe exacerbations than traditional separate SABA reliever strategies, and real-world network meta-analysis confirms the benefit in populations trial criteria exclude. Implementation demands patient education — the inhaler counts as both preventer and reliever — but converts asthma care from two-inhaler complexity to a single consistent message: treat symptoms early, and every treatment is treatment.

teaching_points.claim: SMART uses a single ICS-formoterol inhaler for daily maintenance and as-needed relief, embedding anti-inflammatory treatment in every reliever dose.
ICS-formoterol as controller-and-reliever is associated with significantly fewer severe asthma exacerbations than SABA-reliever-based regimens across severity strata.
Network meta-analysis of real-world populations (often trial-ineligible) confirms SMART's exacerbation benefit beyond RCT settings.

The as-needed-ICS principle generalises: anti-inflammatory reliever therapy (SMART or ICS-containing reliever variants) treats the underlying inflammation, not just bronchospasm — a conceptual break from SABA-only rescue.

uncertainties: Which patients do best on SMART versus MART-naive step-up pathways, and long-term steroid exposure comparisons, need further data.
SMART implementation in health systems with formulary constraints remains uneven.

page.mentor_intro: The inherited arrhythmia syndromes — long QT, Brugada, CPVT, ARVC — are rare conditions where a single missed diagnosis is a young sudden death, and a single over-diagnosis is a lifetime of restriction. Each has a signature trigger: exertion and emotion for long QT and CPVT, rest and fever for Brugada, competitive sport for ARVC. Diagnosis blends ECG patterns, exercise testing, drug challenge, and genetics — where modern panels increasingly identify pathogenic variants, though variants of uncertain significance complicate counselling. Management combines trigger avoidance, beta-blockade (long QT, CPVT), ICD decisions weighted by risk scores, and family cascade screening.

teaching_points.claim: Each syndrome has characteristic triggers — exertion/emotion in long QT and CPVT, rest/sleep/fever in Brugada, sustained exercise in ARVC — and trigger-specific history-taking drives diagnosis.

Diagnostic work-up combines ECG (including recovery-phase and high-lead recordings), exercise testing, ajmaline/flecainide challenge for Brugada, imaging for ARVC, and genetic testing with informed counselling.
Beta-blockade (preferably non-selective, e.g. nadolol/propranolol) is foundational for long QT and CPVT; ICDs are reserved for high-risk profiles given device-related harms in young patients.
Exercise recommendations are syndrome-specific and increasingly individualised; blanket sport bans are giving way to shared decisions weighing relative risk and psychological benefit.

uncertainties: Risk-stratification for ICD in Brugada and ARVC remains imprecise; programme-shock trade-offs in the young are actively debated.
Management of variants of uncertain significance and genotype-positive/phenotype-negative relatives follows expert consensus rather than trial evidence.
mcq_angles: Trigger-specific history for each syndrome.
Diagnostic tests: drug challenge, exercise ECG, genetics.
Beta-blocker selection and ICD thresholds.

page.mentor_intro: The COURAGE-era question — should stable coronary disease get stents first or medicine first? — was substantially answered by ISCHEMIA: in stable patients without left-main disease, an initial invasive strategy did not reduce hard events compared with conservative management with optimal medical therapy, though symptom relief favoured revascularisation in angina-heavy patients. The clinical translation is a triage skill: left-main, severe proximal multivessel with impaired function, and refractory symptoms despite medical therapy point to the cath lab; everything else starts with optimal medical therapy — antiplatelets, statins, beta-blockade, risk-factor control — and escalates by symptoms, not by stenosis percentages alone.

teaching_points.claim: In stable coronary disease without left-main or equivalent anatomy, an initial conservative strategy with optimal medical therapy is event-equivalent to routine invasive management (ISCHEMIA-era evidence).
Revascularisation retains clear roles: left-main disease, proximal multivessel disease with reduced function, and symptom relief when angina persists despite medical therapy.

Optimal medical therapy is itself prognostic: antiplatelet therapy, high-intensity statins, blood-pressure and glycaemic control, beta-blockers for angina, and smoking cessation modify outcomes independent of revascularisation.
Symptom burden, not stenosis percentage alone, should drive escalation decisions in stable disease; ischaemia-guided selection refines who benefits from the cath lab.

uncertainties: Long-term (>10 year) outcomes of initial conservative versus invasive strategies are still accumulating.
Whether modern high-risk plaque imaging should redirect patients to early revascularisation is under study.

page.mentor_intro: Inotropes buy time in shock at a price: increased myocardial oxygen demand, arrhythmias, and — in the dopamine tradition — harm shown in trials. The modern grammar: norepinephrine is the vasopressor backbone of cardiogenic shock (renin-angiotensin support with the least tachyarrhythmia), dobutamine adds inotropy when output remains inadequate, and levosimendan or milrinone offer phosphodiesterase/calcium-sensitising alternatives without catecholamine load. Epinephrine and dopamine are de-emphasised after outcome signals. Inotropes are a bridge — to revascularisation, recovery, or temporary mechanical support — not a destination; the toughest modern skill is recognising when they merely prolong dying.

teaching_points.claim: Norepinephrine is the first-line vasopressor in cardiogenic shock, providing peripheral vascular support with less tachycardia and arrhythmia than dopamine or epinephrine.

Dobutamine is the standard inotrope add-on for low cardiac output; its beta-agonism increases contractility at the cost of oxygen demand and arrhythmia risk, warranting ECG and filling-pressure monitoring.

Non-catecholamine options — levosimendan (calcium sensitiser, active metabolites) and milrinone (PDE-3 inhibitor) — suit catecholamine-resistant or beta-blocked patients but cause vasodilatation and hypotension.
Inotropes and vasopressors bridge to definitive therapy — revascularisation, recovery, or escalation to temporary mechanical circulatory support in refractory shock.

uncertainties: Whether levosimendan improves outcomes over dobutamine in cardiogenic shock remains unproven at trial level.
Optimal timing and patient selection for mechanical support escalation is centre-dependent and incompletely evidence-based.
mcq_angles: Vasopressor selection in cardiogenic shock and why dopamine lost favour.
Dobutamine pharmacology, monitoring, and arrhythmia risk.

page.mentor_intro: Fasting hypoglycaemia with endogenous hyperinsulinaemia is insulinoma until proven otherwise: the classic diagnostic triad (Whipple's) of symptoms with low glucose, relief with glucose, and — from the supervised 72-hour fast — inappropriately elevated insulin, C-peptide, and proinsulin during hypoglycaemia. The C-peptide is the discriminator that splits the differential: endogenous hyperinsulinaemia (insulinoma, sulfonylurea use) versus exogenous insulin (C-peptide suppressed) and IGF-2-mediated hypoglycaemia. Definitive treatment is surgical resection after localisation — the majority are benign solitary adenomas — with medical bridging (diazoxide, frequent feeds) for the unresectable minority.

teaching_points.claim: The supervised 72-hour fast is the reference diagnostic test: symptomatic hypoglycaemia with inappropriately elevated insulin, C-peptide, and proinsulin confirms endogenous hyperinsulinemic hypoglycaemia.

C-peptide and insulin antibodies discriminate the causes: elevated C-peptide indicates insulinoma or sulfonylurea ingestion; suppressed C-peptide indicates exogenous insulin; insulin antibodies suggest autoimmune hypoglycaemia.
Sulfonylurea screen (blood or urine) is essential before attributing hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia to insulinoma; the biochemical profiles overlap.
Treatment of choice is surgical resection of the localised lesion (most insulinomas are benign and solitary); preoperative localisation and intraoperative glucose monitoring guide the operation.

uncertainties: Localisation strategy for occult insulinomas (multiphasic CT, MRI, endoscopic ultrasound, selective arterial calcium stimulation) follows centre algorithms without comparative-trial evidence.
Management of malignant or metastatic insulinoma (diazoxide, everolimus, peptide-receptor therapy) is individualised.

page.mentor_intro: Insulin prescribing is applied pharmacokinetics: the basal insulins (glargine, detemir, degludec) provide flat, peakless coverage tuned by duration — degludec's ultra-long profile smoothing day-to-day variability — while prandial analogues (lispro, aspart, glulisine) peak fast and clear quickly to match meals. Premixed and co-formulated products trade flexibility for simplicity: fixed ratios suit predictable routines and limited self-management capacity, at the cost of adjustment granularity. Switching between types — the commonest real-world manoeuvre — requires attention to unit-for-unit conversion caveats, overlap timing, and hypoglycaemia vigilance in the transition window.

teaching_points.claim: Basal analogues (glargine, detemir, degludec) provide flat 24-hour-plus coverage; degludec's duration beyond 42 hours confers the lowest day-to-day glucose variability and some dosing-time flexibility.
Prandial analogues (lispro, aspart, glulisine) mimic physiologic meal peaks with rapid onset and short duration; they are dosed with meals and allow flexible carbohydrate matching.

Co-formulations such as insulin degludec/insulin aspart (70/30) combine basal stability with prandial coverage in a single injection — the two components retain their individual pharmacokinetic profiles.

Premixed insulins suit patients with regular meals and limited self-management capacity, but the fixed ratio prevents independent titration of basal versus prandial components — a key switching consideration.

uncertainties: Whether ultra-long basal analogues reduce severe hypoglycaemia enough to justify cost over glargine varies by population and setting.
Optimal conversion ratios when switching between basal analogues or to co-formulations are partly empiric.

page.mentor_intro: Insulin pump therapy — continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion — delivers basal-bolus physiology without injections, and its modern form is converging with continuous glucose monitoring into hybrid closed-loop systems that algorithmically adjust delivery. Candidate selection matters more than the hardware: motivated patients (or parents) able to count carbohydrates, troubleshoot occlusions, and manage the device unlock the benefit; system complexity without skills produces the same glycaemia with more failure modes. Sick-day rules complete the picture: illness, ketones, and pump interruption demand proactive sick-day insulin strategies and never omitting basal insulin — pump suspension plus illness is the classic route to DKA.

teaching_points.claim: CSII provides continuous basal infusion with bolus dosing for meals, enabling precise insulin delivery matched to lifestyle; systematic-review evidence supports glycaemic benefit over multiple daily injections in appropriate patients.

Hybrid closed-loop systems link CGM to algorithm-driven basal adjustment, reducing hypoglycaemia and improving time-in-range; systematic review and economic analysis support adoption in type 1 diabetes.
Patient selection is the rate-limiting step: carbohydrate-counting ability, device-competence, motivation, and support structure predict success better than any device feature.

Sick-day rules are safety-critical: never omit insulin during illness, monitor glucose and ketones frequently, have an injection backup plan for pump failure, and seek urgent care for vomiting with ketones.

uncertainties: Fully closed-loop (unannounced-meal) systems and their real-world performance are maturing.
Cost-effectiveness thresholds for hybrid closed-loop across health systems are still being established.
